title: A Shift in Your Leadership Mindset Is Critical for Promotion
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article describes a mindset shift that senior leaders look for before promoting someone: moving from purely 'representative leadership,' where a manager advocates almost exclusively for their own team, toward a more institutional view that weighs the whole enterprise. It notes that leaders who never make this shift are frequently the ones passed over for advancement, because those above them are watching whether the person's questions and concerns are expanding beyond their direct reports. The piece connects this to the familiar advice to 'act as if you already are in the seat,' explaining that concretely means engaging with enterprise-level metrics and issues before being asked to. It concludes that leaders who stay locked into a purely representative mindset limit both their value and their promotability.
points: Early-career leaders naturally adopt a 'representative' mindset, advocating mainly for their own team.
Promotion typically requires a shift toward weighing broader institutional and enterprise interests.
Senior leaders watch whether a person's focus expands beyond their direct reports before promoting them.
'Acting the next role' concretely means engaging with enterprise-level metrics and issues in advance.
Staying stuck in a purely representative mindset can cap both value delivered and career advancement.
quotes: How leaders think of themselves and what role they play in an organization shapes much of their everyday leadership.
We might call this representative leadership for the obvious reason that the leader acts for those they lead.
Leaders who are overlooked for promotion have often failed to make this shift.
Senior leaders have more confidence in the future when the newly promoted leader has their eyes focused upward on the bigger issues.
How a leader “acts the next role” is by becoming more expansive in what matters.
This prevents them from adding the value they are capable of and often negates their ability to be promoted.
